This section examines predictions from the bilepton model, an extension of the standard model where the gauge group shifts from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3) \times U(1)$ and fermion families are arranged non-sequentially, with the third family differing from the first two. To satisfy the requirements for triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom, the model necessitates exactly three families. The anticipated new physics comprises bileptons and three heavy quarks, ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. While QCD will bind these heavy quarks with light quarks and among themselves to create baryons and mesons, these composite particles will remain undetectable at the LHC but could be observed at a hypothetical 100 TeV proton-proton collider, unlike the bileptons. The section concludes with predictions regarding these baryons and mesons. As with other beyond-Standard-Model scenarios, this framework also generates predictions for neutral meson mixing and flavor-changing processes involving the light quarks.

This paper introduces IDET systems grounded in SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM, serving as the counterparts to our optimal wideband waveforming approach detailed in [1]. We formulate optimization problems aimed at maximizing both fair-throughput and sum-throughput. Leveraging a fixed-point based alternating algorithm, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput solutions for both SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM configurations. Furthermore, we develop a near-optimal, low-complexity algorithm to address these issues within the LUT-OFDM domain. The end-to-end fair-throughput and sum-throughput for each configuration are calculated via a binary search method to determine the target mutual information per subcarrier, followed by an entropy maximization algorithm to establish the ideal integer power levels for those subcarriers. Simulations comparing the proposed solutions for IDET in ILLUXT-OFDM, LUT-OFDM, and SISO-OFDM/MISO-OFDM demonstrate that the fair-throughput gains of our ILLUXT-OFDM solution over existing approaches exceed those achieved by the gain improvements of our optimal wideband idefet in multi-carrier OFDM systems. These results highlight the value of our optimal wideband idefet framework for evaluating future IDET system architectures. Additionally, we observe that increasing the number of antennas does not necessarily lead to fairness-throughput improvements, as this count must be balanced against the required bandwidth per subcarrier to ensure gains. Finally, the simulations confirm the practical viability of our ideal wideband idefet algorithm by showing minimal fairness-throughput losses when moving from the ILLUXT-OFDM setup to the optimal wideband idefet configuration.

Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) demands a unified framework that integrates extensive datasets from both theoretical predictions and experimental data. While data integration primarily involves standardizing formats, incorporating theoretical predictions is more complex due to the involvement of multiple components. Various independent groups develop distinct providers for different processes, utilizing diverse input parameters (runcards) and output structures (interpolation grids). Furthermore, because processes are measured across different scales, the PDF candidate requires DGLAP evolution, either calculated dynamically or precomputed into grids. Our goal is to automate all these steps within a single framework, making it a valuable resource for any PDF fitting group and potentially for broader phenomenological investigations. Although not designed as a general-purpose physics simulation tool, this framework could also assist in processing predictions for other processes outside the scope of standard PDF fits. To date, no open-source software has covered all necessary components, but our new tool, called Ladybug, achieves this completeness. We have demonstrated Ladybug's capabilities with a successful global fit of CT18+ electrons using a comprehensive dataset set, and the code is now accessible at https://github.com/cteq/ladybug. Complementary to Ladybug, a smaller utility named Unwinder handles the conversion of other PDF providers into compatible interpolation grids.

This research conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent methane-air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them well-suited for linearizing to predict reactions to acoustic forcing. These predictions were generated using the commercial RANS code STAR-CCM+, which utilizes the Real $k$-$\epsilon$ model. The resulting linear operator was then analyzed to examine responses to upstream actuation. Results indicate that both mean flow and heat release oscillate when excited acoustically, with heat release fluctuations primarily occurring in the shear layer due to incident acoustic wave fluctuations. Furthermore, the response to forced oscillations aligns well with responses to uniform excitation, confirming the superposition principle. Finally, these findings regarding acoustic forcing are compared with observations from actively controlled thermoacoustic combustors.

Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated relation, a specific nonlocal model is developed to investigate the accelerated expansion of the universe. The model's parameters are constrained by fitting the nonlocal term to an effective field theory description, which itself is calibrated against cosmological observations. Furthermore, a generalized version of this model is created to address other phenomena, such as the deflection of light by gravity.

The detection of certain variable X-ray sources in the Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date. These findings indicate that the existence of a neutron star LMXB population capable of accounting for the $R$ and $N1$ source variability is unlikely given current observations, unless future X-ray monitors with greater sensitivity detect more frequent outbursts from known systems or a new, highly active system is discovered in the Galactic Centre. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the formation channels of such binaries and the potential existence of black hole LMXBs.

Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two separate sets of entities. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Additionally, for the specific case of a complete bipartite graph, we establish that a planar embedding after splitting $V$ vertices involves roughly $3V/2$ remaining crossings, indicating that further reductions would require splitting additional vertices. Finally, we adapted our algorithm to handle book embeddings, seeking to minimize crossings between edges when represented on $p$ pages.

Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial complement to side-channel attacks. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel method that integrates prior strategies with simultaneous multithreading (SMT) architectures. Beyond this new technique, we identify a previously unrecognized source of slowdown by analyzing cache eviction as a root cause. The resulting performance degradation is substantially greater than previous methods, thereby enhancing the time granularity available for Flush+Reload attacks. We evaluated HyperDegrade across various Intel microarchitectures, achieving significant slowdowns that, in specific microbenchmark scenarios, represent a three-order-of-magnitude improvement over state-of-the-art solutions. To assess the effectiveness of performance degradation in amplifying side channels, we introduced and validated specific leakage metrics. Our findings indicate that HyperDegrade improves time granularity without compromising trace quality. Furthermore, we conducted a fair comparison of three performance degradation strategies when paired with Flush+Reload from an attacker's viewpoint. We also devised an attack targeting an underutilized vulnerability in OpenSSL, where HyperDegrade demonstrated superior performance by reducing the number of required Flush+Reload traces needed for success by a factor of three. In terms of cryptographic contributions, we revisited the recently proposed Raccoon attack on TLS-DH key exchanges, extending its application to other protocols. Leveraging HyperDegrade, we constructed an end-to-end attack proving that Raccoon-like exploits can succeed with real data, addressing a gap left by earlier research. Finally, we devised a countermeasure and validated its efficacy through experiments. It is crucial to note that both Raccoon and its associated attack remain viable only when combined with a side-channel exploit; consequently, HyperDegrade is the enabling factor that bridges this final link. To provide broader context, we outlined the circumstances under which Raccoon-like attacks and their mitigations are relevant, delivering a comprehensive analysis of this issue. As HyperDegrade is highly effective against Raccoon, its implications likely extend to other protocols and attacks as well. To broaden the security community's understanding, we concluded by proposing a side-channel attack against Shacal2—a block cipher previously deemed secure against all known practical attacks—to demonstrate the real-world consequences of HyperDegrade. Our experimental results confirm that this attack successfully cryptanalyzed Shacal2, validating the power of performance degradation side channels and the efficacy of HyperDegrade. To further quantify these effects, we defined additional metrics for measuring the impact of performance degradation side channels.

Coordination serves as a vital capability in multi-agent systems, enabling the completion of objectives that single agents cannot achieve alone. This study examines how a team of regular graphs structured around two distinct tasks selects an optimal strategy to maximize collective utility, while acknowledging that communication and computation are constrained by agent-specific limits. We model a scenario involving a social media posting activity and an emergency evacuation, grounded in a game-theoretic framework where agents prioritize individual utility. Our findings demonstrate that when communication costs are high and tasks carry unequal value, the optimal approach involves balancing randomization with deterministic choices. Specifically, agents should randomize their participation based on the relative worth of the tasks. Furthermore, we present a novel hierarchical Nash equilibrium concept, which proves more effective than the traditional Nash equilibrium in specific contexts. This concept guides agents in minimizing information leakage to competitors and optimizing overall utility. These results offer practical insights for real-world applications, including emergency responses and multi-agent marketing efforts. Ultimately, this work provides a game-theoretic analysis of multi-task coordination, delivering actionable strategies for real-world scenarios and highlighting the significance of considering agent limitations and competitive dynamics. This paper demonstrates the embedding of regularly acting groups and diagonal groups into wreath products under their product action by utilizing Cartesian Decomposition. Consequently, when embedding regularly acting groups or diagonal groups, the analysis of the acting variable becomes unnecessary. By employing this technique, we provide a new proof of Theorem 1.1 in reference \cite{S89} regarding the simplicity of certain wreath products, and we offer a novel demonstration that the direct product of two non-abelian simple groups is not simple. Additionally, using this approach, we derive a new proof showing that a specific group is not simple, thereby revealing an alternative mechanism for identifying direct decompositions via the removal of Wreath Product structures. Finally, by incorporating this result with a recent finding of the first author, we conclude that the direct product of non-abelian simple groups lacks a wreath product structure. Ultimately, this outcome constitutes a version of the Simple Group Factors Conjecture. Throughout this work, we also introduce and examine several new concepts and properties related to Cartesian Decomposition and Simple Groups.

The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise and ultimately by optical losses within the signal-recycling cavity. This limitation represents a primary barrier to detecting gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers in both current and future detectors, as it remains independent of arm length and the level of injected squeezing. In this study, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, derived from a Michelson interferometer by optically linking the end mirrors to form an additional cavity. This configuration creates a triply-coupled cavity system capable of surpassing the loss-induced high-frequency limit inherent to signal-recycled Michelson interferometers. Using parameters comparable to advanced LIGO+, a sloshing-Sagnac design could achieve sevenfold improved sensitivity at 2.5 kHz, or a fourfold increase in signal-to-noise ratio for typical post-merger binary neutron star spins. As an evolution of the Michelson architecture, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer offers a viable topology for upgrading current detectors and for future-generation observatories.

Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for delivering ultra-high data rates in environments with high user density. Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationarities and distinct visibility regions (VRs). These factors, combined with high UE density and limited pilot resources, make the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling algorithms particularly difficult. This paper introduces a joint RA and scheduling approach called the non-overlapping VR XL-MIMO (NOVR-XL) protocol. This method leverages the unique VRs of individual UEs to enhance RA performance and prioritizes scheduling UEs with non-overlapping VRs within the same payload data pilot resource. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed scheme yields substantial improvements in sum rate compared to conventional RA methods, while also lowering access latency and overall connectivity performance. The practical viability of this approach is further validated through measurements collected from a real-world 128-antenna deployment.

Looking ahead, using an error localization metric like LIAA (Li Edit Distance for Indian Languages) instead of Levenshtein could yield additional benefits for creating rule-based and informed OCR solutions for Indian elections, as LIAA accounts for Devanagari-specific features such as ligatures and diacritics that Levenshtein does not. This study investigates potential global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere using a simplified General Circulation Model (GCM) derived from the University of Hamburg's Portable University Model for the Atmosphere. The model incorporates simplified linear boundary layer friction, Newtonian cooling, and dry convective adjustment. Through a series of controlled experiments, researchers varied the planetary rotation rate and the imposed equator-to-pole temperature gradient. These variables were converted into dimensionless parameters to define a parameter space where distinct circulation regimes are identified and categorized. Significant trends emerge when altering the planetary rotation rate alongside frictional and thermal relaxation timescales. The progression of circulation regimes with respect to planetary rotation closely mirrors findings from laboratory studies on rotating, stratified fluids, particularly when topographic $\beta$-effects are included. Additionally, a regular baroclinic wave regime appears at intermediate values of both planetary vorticity and thermal relaxation. Reaching super-rotating states requires strong equatorial heating combined with weak frictional and radiative damping. These results support the conclusion that a terrestrial atmosphere under high frictional and radiative damping, coupled with low greenhouse gas concentrations and low cloud cover, would likely exhibit circulation regimes analogous to those observed on the gas giant planets. The dimensionless parameters outlined in this work offer guidance for applying GCMs to atmospheres of exoplanets that possess Earth-like compositions but may have significantly different environmental conditions. These parameters were utilized to guide experiments in a simplified exoplanet GCM, with those efforts detailed in the accompanying paper (Arney et al., 2020).

This study presents a real integral formulation for the reciprocal $\Gamma$ function using a regularized hypersingular integral. It confirms the equivalence between this new form and the standard complex representation, subsequently deriving a regularized complex expression that follows the conventional Hankel contour. These findings offer multiple equivalent representations for both the Gamma and reciprocal Gamma functions, which could prove beneficial when deriving identities involving these functions. The derivation of the regularized complex expression for the reciprocal Gamma function also enables a fresh proof of the factorized complex formula. We introduce a new, compact representation for graphical models, a foundational framework for numerous reasoning tasks. Empirical comparisons between FABE and leading methods for most probable explanation (recursive best-first, structured message passing) and constrained optimization (CPLEX, GUROBI, toulbar2), conducted via a standard methodology, validate the effectiveness of our approach, demonstrating runtime gains of up to five orders of magnitude. Theoretical proofs and additional empirical evidence confirm that our method outperforms existing algorithms for this problem. Finally, we adapted the representation for an open-ended exact algorithm (without heuristics) for most probable explanation under different constraints; the code for this algorithm, along with all others evaluated, is publicly available at https://github.com/GraphicalModels/CPRolexMPE. This study presents a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter that models target birth and undetected target intensities on a grid. Among the most critical hyperparameters for neural networks, the loss function plays a pivotal role, yet selecting the appropriate one remains challenging due to the vast array of available options. Despite this, related studies often fail to provide rigorous justifications for their specific choices, suggesting a dogmatic approach within the deep learning community that lacks empirical grounding. This work investigates supervised classification tasks to evaluate how loss function selection influences training outcomes. Although some functions yield suboptimal results, our empirical analysis demonstrates that underutilized losses, such as KL Divergence, can significantly surpass state-of-the-art alternatives. These findings underscore the necessity of treating the loss function as a tunable hyperparameter rather than adopting it as a fixed default. Ultimately, this research highlights the importance of empirically determining optimal loss functions specific to each dataset and problem, potentially revolutionizing the application of deep learning across computer science and beyond. We introduce ATOMIC, a comprehensive atlas of everyday commonsense reasoning structured through 877,000 textual descriptions of inferential knowledge. To differentiate between causes and effects, agents and themes, voluntary versus involuntary events, and actions versus mental states, we define nine distinct if-then relation types. By generatively training neural models on the rich inferential knowledge within ATOMIC, we demonstrate that these models can acquire basic commonsense abilities and reason about unseen events. Furthermore, experimental findings indicate that multitask models utilizing the hierarchical structure of these if-then relation types achieve more accurate inference than those trained in isolation, a result confirmed by both automated metrics and human evaluation. Ultimately, the extensive inferential knowledge in ATOMIC serves as a valuable dataset for investigating neural models, helping to advance architectures and loss functions designed for commonsense reasoning and related tasks such as natural language inference, natural language understanding, and natural language generation. A graph $G=(V,E)$ equipped with geodesic distance $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ is considered resolved by a non-empty vertex subset $R$ if, for every pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, the condition $d(u,r)=d(v,r)$ holding for all $r\in R$ implies $u=v$. The metric dimension of $G$ corresponds to the size of its minimal resolving set. This manuscript introduces and examines the concepts of resolvability and metric dimension under a truncated geodesic distance defined by a threshold $k$, utilizing the metric $d_k(u,v):=\min\{d(u,v),k+1\}$. We define the metric dimension of $G$ relative to $d_k$ as $\beta_k(G)$. The study analyzes how $\beta_k(G)$ varies with respect to $k$ and the graph's diameter. Furthermore, we characterize the truncated metric dimension for paths, cycles, and graphs exhibiting extreme dimensions, specifically those of order $n$ where $\beta_k(G)=n-2$ or $\beta_k(G)=n-1$. The work concludes with an exploration of several issues concerning the truncated metric dimension of trees. This line of inquiry holds significant value for locating problems, network conglomeration, topological data analysis, and robotics within the context of metric spaces. Specifically, $\beta_k(G)$ serves as a crucial parameter for emergency services, such as fire or police departments, to rapidly identify and navigate towards the origin of an incident along a road network or other metric space, provided the "accuracy" of the information received from distinct locations does not surpass $k$ edges. We support our discussions with various definitions and a collection of lemmas, propositions, and theorems.

This study reports the potential detection of a nonmonotonic radial rotation profile in a low-mass, low-luminosity giant star. While low- and intermediate-mass stars typically exhibit rigid rotation on the main sequence, stellar evolution into the giant phase—characterized by core contraction and envelope expansion—generally predicts a profile with a rapidly rotating core and a slower envelope. KIC 9267654, however, displays evidence of a core rotation period of $\sim$2 days contrasted with an envelope rotation rate at least three times higher than conventional predictions for its physical properties. Angular momentum transport mechanisms, such as gravity-inertial wave braking, meridional circulation, and magnetic tensions, are insufficient to account for this profile. We propose that the accretion of a planet onto the star's surface could account for the anomalously fast rotation. Alternatively, new theories regarding viscosity and turbulence in stellar envelopes are required to explain this low-mass star's rotation profile. The existence of such a profile challenges current understanding of angular momentum conservation during stellar envelope expansion. Otherwise, the star's properties, in particular its microshaking, remain unexplained.

While deep learning models perform well on labeled data for specific events, their efficacy often drops when encountering new events due to domain shifts. Extensive experiments on multimedia datasets from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate that MetaFEND effectively detects fake news in previously unseen events, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. The framework's potential is further validated by a real-world deployment on X (formerly Twitter) to address misinformation surrounding an emerging political event. The source code is available at https://github.com/Pranav-003/Mimic-NET-for-Fake-News-Detection.

Laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) represents a new minimally invasive approach for ablating intracranial structures to manage mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE). Automating lesion quantification through pre- and post-treatment region of interest (ROI) segmentation offers an objective means to evaluate therapeutic efficacy. This framework comprises two sequential networks: a mask synthesis network and a mask-guided lesion synthesis network. To leverage extrinsic information for enhanced supervision, we developed a condition embedding block (CEB) and a mask embedding block (MEB) that encode intrinsic mask characteristics into the feature space. Ultimately, a segmentation network was trained on a combination of raw and synthetic lesion images to assess the framework's efficacy. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach generates realistic synthetic images and significantly improves the performance of downstream segmentation tasks compared to conventional data augmentation methods. Furthermore, the approach integrates both similar and dissimilar samples to harmonize unsupervised and supervised extraction processes. Specifically, the study proposes three methodologies: an unsupervised contrastive learning approach, along with two distinct supervised contrastive learning methods. Extensive numerical experiments conducted across five real-world datasets confirm that the proposed framework outperforms existing methods. Additionally, the study concludes with a detailed analysis of the introduced contrastive learning-based approaches.

Although large language models (LLMs) achieve human-level performance across many natural language tasks, it remains unclear whether they absorb knowledge more effectively from structured sources like knowledge graphs (KGs) or from unstructured text. This study introduces a technique to embed structured knowledge into LLMs by directly training T5 models on factual triples extracted from knowledge graphs. Our results demonstrate that T5 models pre-trained on Wikidata using this approach surpass standard baselines on FreebaseQA, WikiHop, and specific subsets of TriviaQA and NaturalQuestions. Furthermore, models trained on factual triples perform comparably to those trained on natural language sentences containing identical information. When applied to the smaller WikiMovies dataset, our method achieved a threefold increase in exact match scores on the MetaQA task relative to the T5 baseline. A key benefit of this approach is that it eliminates the need for aligning knowledge graphs with text corpora during data preparation, rendering it especially advantageous for industry-scale knowledge graphs. The analysis reveals that, under specific conditions, the shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature (or pressure) exhibit non-monotonic behaviors. Furthermore, from the perspective of the shadow radius, the phase transition temperature is higher than that derived from the horizon radius under identical conditions. Finally, the influence of the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter on both the shadow radius and thermal profiles is further explored. The underlying physical mechanisms regarding the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter's effect on the shadow radius and thermal profiles are also discussed. This work underscores that the black hole shadow acts as a potent tool for investigating the fundamental properties of black holes. The relevant figures are available from the author.

Our findings suggest that this entanglement-switching protocol within tomograms can serve as a detection tool in quantum communication scenarios, potentially offering advantages over traditional Wiener-Chirp-based methods.

This study tackles the persistent challenge of extracting dynamical information from noisy acoustic emission signals generated by an adhesive tape being peeled under a constant traction velocity. By applying a phase space reconstruction method, we confirm deterministic chaotic dynamics through the identification of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent within a specific range of traction speeds. These findings are interpreted using a model that underscores the deterministic nature of acoustic emissions by linking them to stick-slip dynamics. Additionally, we document the emergence of periodicity at low speeds and chaos at high speeds, analyzing these transitions in light of a recently proposed fractal scaling law for acoustic emissions across varying traction speeds. The correlation dimension and a newly defined dynamical order parameter are examined as functions of this fractal scaling parameter to support the underlying mechanical mechanism. While these results pertain to an adhesive tape, the identified deterministic dynamics and the proposed mechanical model have broader implications for understanding crackling noise in other systems. Consequently, this research contributes to the investigation of deterministic chaos in one-dimensional frictional systems exhibiting stick-slip behavior, such as blocks on inclined planes, and highlights the significance of the correlation dimension and Lyapunov exponent in determining the onset of chaos in related systems. The reported periodic and chaotic dynamics, along with their associated fractal scaling, may also aid in detecting phase transitions in other systems that exhibit crackling noise. Specifically, the transition from chaotic to deterministic dynamics observed in this work at low traction speeds could serve as an indicator of a crisis-induced transition from chaotic to periodic behavior in systems displaying crackling noise under constant force, such as the well-known Burridge-Knopoff model. Such a detection mechanism was experimentally verified in a different system involving granular matter under constant compression. Ultimately, this study provides evidence for deterministic chaotic dynamics and a corresponding mechanical mechanism in an adhesive tape, a finding with potential applications in other materials, as demonstrated by recent investigations on brittle solids. Such applications will become feasible if the deterministic dynamics identified here and the mechanical model proposed for the tape can be adapted to other materials, for instance, by accounting for the fact that a tape's acoustic emissions result from tearing rather than fracturing. Furthermore, the mechanical model could be extended to explain the coexistence of different emission sources (tearing, bubbling, and friction) observed during the peeling of a low-ducktape under constant velocity, a phenomenon that remains unexplained. Complementary to this mechanical model, the determination of a positive Lyapunov exponent indicates that the acoustic emissions of an adhesive tape under constant traction velocity are deterministic chaotic.

This article updates the definition of the angle function to accommodate a broader class of spaces characterized by a betweenness relation, which we consider a more natural framework. Within this generalized setting, we resolve both problems originally posed by Menger. Furthermore, we establish an alternative characterization of the angle function that does not rely on the betweenness relation; using this feature, we provide a solution to an auxiliary problem also discussed by Menger. Throughout this work, the concept of an "infinitesimally Euclidean" space—introduced by the authors in a prior article—is utilized multiple times. Historically, such spaces were investigated in the 1930s by Menger and others as a method to prove the existence of a global angle function. Today, these ideas have been revisited in the context of non-Archimedean manifolds. Finally, we sketch an outline of how the problems from this paper and those addressed by Menger in the 1930s can be solved when the underlying spaces are non-Archimedean metric spaces.

Neural network-based models applied to point clouds, such as PointNet and its variants, have achieved success in specific domains like automotive LiDAR processing. However, deploying these models in real-world scenarios remains challenging due to the high training costs associated with deep learning. To address this, this paper introduces Transformation Specific Smoothing (TPC), a post-hoc method that enhances robustness against geometric transformations, including rotation and scaling. By integrating task-specific prior knowledge of point cloud transformations (TP), TPC achieves significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art posterior smoothing techniques. This gain is particularly evident when increasing the magnitude of geometric perturbations. As a non-training based approach, TPC offers a cost-effective solution suitable for various point cloud models and diverse real-world deployment situations. The code for our implementation is accessible at https://github.com/rajivksharma/TPC. We anticipate that TPC will benefit a wide range of real-world applications involving point cloud data.

The verification techniques of formal methods are now being applied to program testing, with the goal of enhancing the reliability of software development, testing, and evolution. Our geometric theory of testing serves as the specification for a testing environment, which functions as the final stage of a toolchain designed to assist professional developers, hobbyists, and computer science students. This environment features an automated algorithm that identifies errors within executed tests and guides their correction by displaying a stick diagram of causal execution chains on a screen. Users can navigate this diagram backward, similar to using a satnav to follow roads on a map, which highlights the specific locations in the code that require modification to eliminate the error. Furthermore, the environment provides an automated algorithm that generates a certificate—a stick diagram of the entire execution chain—confirming once the erroneous error has been resolved. At this point, the certificate also reveals any remaining issues. Our environment has already been utilized by computer science students and professionals to train themselves in the skills required to write correct code. Additionally, the automated algorithms for directing error correction and generating errorlessness certificates can be integrated into existing professional testing tools to enrich their functionality. The verification algorithms responsible for the error-directed correction algorithm and the errorlessness certificate algorithm constitute the core of a proof system dedicated to causal reasoning. This system of proof rules, which has been established comprehensively, offers a set of rules for reasoning about causal chains (sequences of events) that can be incorporated into other proof systems, such as those used for validating safety arguments in safety-critical systems. Such rules could be employed to automate parts of the process for discharging proof obligations related to error traces found by executors, like those identified by static analysis tools. Finally, the algorithms for error-directed correction and errorlessness generation can be incorporated into the tool supporting the "correct by construction" development methodology (which comprises said methodology and its associated toolchain) to serve as a final validation algorithm for a candidate correct program. This would help establish the program's errorlessness (the absence of runtime errors), thereby providing evidence for its semantic property of correctness when combined with assumptions from its specification and liveness properties. Consequently, these algorithms could be integrated into the toolchain for the correct-by-construction methodology as evidence supporting a program's correctness. This paper presents an explicit formulation of the weight component of Serre's conjecture for GL_2, grounded in Kummer theory and deliberately avoiding p-adic Hodge theory. The approach relies on characterizing the reduction modulo p of crystalline extensions via specific "G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles" and applying Abrashkin's result, which relates these cocycles to Kummer theory. While Dembele-Diamond-Roberts previously offered an explicit formulation using local class field theory (for the unramified case) and the second author did so in the general case, we demonstrate that their description can be derived directly from ours through the explicit reciprocity laws established by Brueckner, Shafarevich, and Vostokov. These computations highlight how our reliance on Kummer theory sidesteps specific combinatorial complexities found in those earlier works. Furthermore, we provide a simplified proof of the functional equation for the Euler characteristic of the second author's cocycles. Although this result was originally utilized by the second author merely to fix normalization issues in that specific cocycle, our explicit computations reveal that the equation is actually essential for the broader application of these cocycles. Finally, we sketch potential directions for generalizing this framework to higher dimensions.

Fiber-reinforced composites featuring nanofiller-modified polymer matrices hold significant promise for enhancing the safety of high-risk engineering structures. These materials possess an inherent self-sensing capability, as their electrical conductivity alters in response to deformation and damage. This phenomenon, termed piezoresistivity, has been widely utilized for damage detection through electrical resistance measurements and tomographic imaging methods like electrical impedance tomography (EIT). While these approaches are highly effective at identifying the existence of damage, they struggle to deliver accurate details regarding the damage's shape, dimensions, or underlying mechanism. This limitation is especially problematic for laminated composites, which are prone to complex failure modes such as delaminations that are challenging to identify. To address this, we introduce a novel method for precisely determining the shape and size of damage in self-sensing composites. Our approach combines a genetic algorithm with realistic physics-based damage models to reconstruct accurate damage geometry from conductivity variations captured via EIT. We experimentally validated this technique using carbon nanofiber (CNF)-reinforced glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates, focusing on two specific damage mechanisms: through-holes and delaminations. The results demonstrate that this new method can accurately reconstruct multiple through-holes with radii as small as 1.25 mm and delaminations resulting from low-velocity impacts. These findings indicate that integrating piezoresistivity with conductivity-based spatial imaging and physics-based inversion strategies can enable precise damage shape reconstruction in self-sensing composite structures.

We introduce a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces that prioritizes geometric vectors, validating this approach within two-dimensional and three-dimensional spaces. This formulation offers an alternative to the traditional tensor calculus used in Euclidean spaces, one that explicitly highlights vectorial characteristics. Consequently, this method provides a useful pedagogical tool for teaching tensor analysis in Euclidean, Minkowski, and general curved manifolds. By emphasizing the vector nature of these spaces, this approach facilitates the comparison of Euclidean and Minkowski spaces and supports the development of a similar framework for curved manifolds that underscores the distinction between tangent and cotangent vectors. Ultimately, this perspective aids in clarifying the confusion surrounding the equivalence of contravariant and covariant tensors in Euclidean and Minkowski spaces as well as in curved manifolds. Complementary to this, we provide a formulation for Euclidean, Minkowski, and curved spaces that stresses the differentiation between tangent and cotangent vectors. Additionally, we demonstrate how to construct an orthonormal contravariant basis tensor from an orthonormal set of contravariant vector tensors in both Euclidean and Minkowski spaces.

We demonstrate that if a right-angled Artin group $A(\Gamma)$ admits a non-trivial, minimal action on a tree $T$ that is not a line, then $\Gamma$ must contain a separating subgraph $\Lambda$ for which $A(\Lambda)$ stabilizes an edge in $T$. Consequently, all minimal actions of $A(\Gamma)$ on trees are either trivial or stabilize at an edge. Furthermore, we explicitly characterize when an right-angled Artin group possesses a "exotic" action on a tree. As applications, we derive new restrictions on the outer automorphism groups of right-angled Artin groups and establish additional splitting results. Notably, we prove that no right-angled Catellani group whose diagram is not a path can exhibit an exotic action on a right-angled Catellani group's diagram. These findings yield fresh insights into the rigidity of such groups. Our approaches primarily involve explicitly constructing these exotic actions and leveraging the now-extensive theory of Minahan's work on the same topic.

Advancements in technology have enabled big data processing, yet this has created substantial computational challenges when solving large-scale linear systems or performing matrix inversions. Consequently, there has been significant research into fast, approximate iterative methods for matrix inversion accelerated by Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), offering viable alternatives where traditional direct inversion methods are too costly. Existing techniques include the Neumann Series (NS), Newton iteration (NI), Chebyshev Iteration (CI), and Successive Over-Relaxation. This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm derived from the NS, termed "Nested Neumann" (NN). This approach generalizes higher-order iterations of NI and CI by leveraging a computationally efficient iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, dependent on a specified "inception depth." Mathematical analysis confirms that the NN method is globally convergent, with its convergence rate determined by the inception depth and the spectral radius of the preconditioning matrix. Furthermore, the NN iteration exhibits an effective complexity of O(c \times n^2 / 728) per step, where n represents the total matrix elements and c denotes the inception depth. Additionally, an adaptiveNN variant is proposed to dynamically optimize the inception depth and preconditioning matrix during computation. Comparative experiments among NS, NI, CI, successive over-relaxation, NN, and adaptiveNN demonstrate that NN and adaptiveNN achieve the fastest convergence. Specifically, relative to the next best method, NN is approximately 33 times faster with an inception depth of 2 and up to 174 times faster with an inception depth of 7. These results indicate that the NN method and its adaptations represent a significant advancement in iterative, constant-complexity algorithms for fast, approximate large-scale matrix inversion. The source code for NN is accessible at https://github.com/deepinder/NestedNeumann.

Contextual linear bandits represent a theoretically significant model with extensive practical utility, recently attracting considerable attention in wireless applications where communication constraints often limit performance, particularly when contexts exist in a high-dimensional $d$-dimensional space. This paper addresses a distributed memoryless contextual linear bandit learning scenario where agents observe contexts and select actions, yet are geographically separated from the central learner who performs the optimization without direct access to the contexts. Assuming contexts follow a specific distribution, we introduce a method requiring approximately $5d$ bits per context when the distribution is unknown, and zero bits per context if it is known. This approach achieves a regret bound nearly identical to that of a fully observable setting. Specifically, the bound for the unknown distribution case improves upon existing results by a $\log(T)$ factor (where $T$ is the time horizon), while the bound for the known distribution case reaches information-theoretic tightness. These findings hold under the assumption that contexts are mix Gaussian distributed. Numerical experiments confirm that this new approach significantly outperforms standard baselines. To the best of our knowledge, this work constitutes the first study to examine in-depth the constraints imposed by context distributions on the optimal regret bound in contextual bandits. Furthermore, the proposed method is easily adaptable to scenarios where contexts are not Gaussian distributed but can be efficiently encoded and decoded; in such cases, the bound aligns with that of mean-square error compression, indicating that the result is essentially tight. The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism dependent on rapid gas cooling, potentially active in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. This study employs linear analysis to quantify the VSI growth rate in detail, incorporating a model for dust evolution. We demonstrate that dust growth and settling can halt the VSI at ann radii exceeding 3 cm, 6 cm, and 18 cm, contingent upon the initial dust spectrum. Our findings suggest that VSI-driven turbulence could help account for the high  $^{29}$O/ $^{31}$O ratio observed by ALMA in the AS-20 disk, an anomaly difficult to explain without VSI activity. Furthermore, our results indicate that the significant $^{29}$Si/enriched silane gas ratios detected in the outer regions of the ORION-IL7 disk by laboratory-spectroscopy-led observations from the NOEMA array can also be attributed to VSI-induced cooling. Lastly, we conclude that the vertical shear instability may serve as a universal mechanism for enhancing diffusion in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks before dust evolution fully suppresses it. To investigate the specific details of this process within the AS-20 and ORION-IL7 disks, we will conduct such an analysis in the future. (This article refers to List of Figures 0).

This study examines harmonic functions defined on gradient shrinking Ricci solitons that possess constant scalar curvature. We establish a Liouville theorem without relying on gradient estimates, demonstrating that any bounded harmonic function must be constant on such solitons. These findings are significant for analyzing the long-term behavior of harmonic maps. As an application, we prove that any steady 4-solenoidal shrinking soliton in dimension 4 must be gradient. Conversely, we show that no gradient shrinking soliton of the form $M^{4}=\Sigma_{1}\times\Sigma_{2}$, where $\Sigma_{1}$ and $\Sigma_{2}$ are surfaces of genus at least 2, can exist. These results imply that the dimension of the base $B$ cannot exceed 4 for any steady 4-solenoidal shrinking soliton $M^{4}$. Furthermore, we confirm that any shrinking soliton of constant scalar curvature in dimension 4 with non-negative sectional curvature must be steady. These discoveries align with recent work by Cabezas-Rivas and Perelman \cite{CRP}. Additionally, we prove that any steady 5-solenoidal shrinking soliton in dimension 5 with constant scalar curvature must be gradient. We conclude by outlining several open problems related to these areas. The rise of outsourced training and machine learning as a service has introduced new attack vectors, specifically backdoor attacks. These attacks conceal a secret function within a neural network that activates only when a specific trigger is present in the input. While most existing literature assumes static triggers with fixed locations and patterns—properties upon which many detection mechanisms rely—recent studies have demonstrated that image classification countermeasures like Neural Cleanse and ABS can be circumvented using dynamic triggers that remain effective regardless of their position or appearance. However, such dynamic backdoors are resource-intensive, typically requiring a substantial portion of poisoned training data. This work presents the first demonstration that dynamic backdoor attacks can occur via a global average pooling layer without needing an increased volume of poisoned data. Despite this theoretical possibility, experimental results across sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification indicate that implementing such attacks remains highly challenging in practice. Finally, we introduce a novel detection mechanism designed to identify dynamic backdoor attacks during a pre-deployment testing phase, where the defender has access to unpooled poisoned inputs.

This work addresses the challenge of a Parameter Server (PS) learning a model from data distributed across graph nodes, with Federated Learning (FL) serving as the primary application. A significant hurdle in FL is the communication bottleneck between nodes and the PS. Although performing multiple local updates per iteration before syncing with the PS is a common strategy to alleviate this bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of node-specific data often results in biased models and delayed convergence. To overcome both communication and data heterogeneity issues, we investigate Random Walk (RW) learning algorithms. These algorithms utilize direct connections between nodes, which are typically more efficient than communicating with the PS. In this framework, the model acts as a "baton" passed iteratively to a neighboring node after each update. Designing effective RW algorithms is complicated by data heterogeneity and uncertainty regarding data distributions; ideally, nodes with more informative data should be visited more frequently. We formulate this as a sleeping multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem to develop a near-optimal node sampling strategy that minimizes gradient estimate variance and asymptotically approaches optimal sampling. Building on this, we propose an adaptive random walk learning algorithm and provide theoretical convergence guarantees. Our numerical experiments confirm these theoretical results and demonstrate that our algorithm surpasses existing random walk methods. As a concluding practical application, we adapt the algorithm for Federated Learning and show its effectiveness in mitigating bottlenecks caused by data heterogeneity. Furthermore, we apply it to a real-world scenario involving a news recommendation model on a news sharing graph. The proposed method is open-source and available at https://github.com/PrasanthNair/Walk_for_Learning. Keywords: Federated Learning, Random Walk, Heterogeneous Data, Multi-Armed Bandit, Communication Bottleneck, Convergence Rate, News Recommendation Model.

Pixel-level annotation scarcity remains a significant challenge in medical image segmentation. To address this, we present a novel regularization approach utilizing interpolation-based mixing for semi-supervised medical image segmentation. This method employs a consistency regularization strategy that ensures the segmentation of interpolated pairs of unlabeled images aligns with the interpolation of their corresponding segmentation maps. As a form of data-adaptive regularization, it helps reduce overfitting to labeled data, particularly when confidence levels are high. Compared to adversarial and generative models, this approach offers the advantage of requiring no extra computational resources. Evaluations on two public MRI datasets, ACDC and MMWHS, show that our method outperforms existing semi-supervised models. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/hritam-98/ICT-MedSeg. We hope this simple yet effective method provides a valuable baseline for future research in semi-supervised medical image segmentation. Although this study focuses on medical images, the approach is universally applicable and can be tested on other datasets. In summary, this is a consistency-based regularization method designed to improve pixel-wise segmentation masks on unlabeled medical images by ensuring the segmentation of mixed unlabeled images matches the consistency of their respective class segmentation maps. Key techniques include data augmentation, interpolation, and medical image analysis. While iterative methods and adversarial approaches exist for similar tasks, this work distinguishes itself through an interpolation-based consistency regularization framework. Although semi-supervised learning is commonly used in NLP, this research specifically targets medical image segmentation. Furthermore, the model does not employ graph neural networks, natural language processing, or attention mechanisms; its primary innovations are the interpolation-based consistency regularization, the absence of domain-specific fine-tuning, and its utility in handling data privacy concerns. Future work could explore applying this method to other computer vision tasks, as this study is specifically confined to medical image segmentation. By offering a simple, end-to-end solution that needs no additional modules or modules, this research provides a practical baseline for future studies in this area. Potential applications range from general semi-supervised learning to specific domains like medical segmentation, privacy preservation, and computer vision, though this study specifically demonstrates its efficacy in medical image segmentation. Potential future directions include further evaluating this end-to-end semi-supervised model across different computer vision and medical imaging datasets. In clinical settings, this approach could help manage labeled and unlabeled medical images, although its specific utility in surgical planning or remote patient monitoring was not the focus of this work. At the 1927 Solvay conference, Einstein proposed a thought experiment aimed at demonstrating the incompleteness of quantum mechanics by leveraging the instantaneous nonlocal consequences of wave function collapse—a phenomenon he termed "spooky action at a distance"—triggered by measurement. This event preceded the famous Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen critique. In this work, we utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous nonlocal nature of wave function collapse, combined with single-particle entanglement, gives rise to the nonlocal effect of steering. During steering, the remote local system appears, post-collapse, to be in a state determined by the specific observable measured on the entangled partner. We show that single-particle entangled states, when expressed in a basis aligned with the collapse induced by observing the spin of a remotely measured entangled particle, exhibit nonlocality. Consequently, the state of the remotely located single particle instantaneously "steers" across space onto the Bloch sphere defined by the observed spin observable. We demonstrate that truly nonlocal single-particle entangled states are essential for the nonlocality of steering and, as evidenced by Bohmian spin, for the nonlocality inherent in Bell inequality violations. Furthermore, we highlight that the nonlocality found in Bohmian spin correlations between two spin-1/2 particles, whose joint system exists in a truly nonlocal entangled Bell state, directly results from the nonlocality present in the true single-particle entanglement of each of the two spins within that Bell state.

Although the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with advanced information technology systems has delivered substantial benefits to Internet of Vehicles (IoV) ecosystems, it has simultaneously amplified security and privacy risks. Consequently, privacy preservation methods have become a focal point in academic research to safeguard IoV data. However, these existing approaches require specific adaptations to align with evolving IoV architectures. Meanwhile, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution for enhancing data privacy and security within IoVs. Concurrently, Blockchain technology offers significant potential through its secure, decentralized, and auditable mechanisms for data recording and sharing. This paper provides a comprehensive survey on the application and implementation of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs. Additionally, it examines potential challenges, proposed solutions, and future research directions associated with these frameworks. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational resource for developing modern Blockchain-Enabled FL solutions to address various data privacy issues and scenarios in IoVs. Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are a potent class of deep neural networks extensively applied to sequence analysis and modeling. Nevertheless, their substantial model size hinders practical deployment, particularly in video recognition tasks involving high-dimensional data. To address this constraint and maximize the potential of LSTMs, this paper introduces an algorithm and hardware co-design strategy for high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, we introduce the FDHT-LSTM, a model based on a fully decomposed hierarchical Tucker (FDHT) structure that maintains high accuracy with ultra-low complexity. To leverage these algorithmic advantages, we designed a specialized hardware architecture capable of executing the FDHT-LSTM efficiently. Through a refined memory access scheme, the hardware supports complex matrix transformations in real-time without access conflicts. Evaluation results demonstrate that both the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the dedicated hardware accelerator deliver superior performance. Compared to state-of-the-art compressed LSTMs, FDHT-LSTM offers order-of-magnitude reductions in model size alongside significant accuracy gains across various video recognition datasets. Furthermore, against the state-of-the-art tensor decomposed hardware accelerator TIE, our FDHT-LSTM architecture achieves higher throughput, better area efficiency, and improved energy efficiency on the LSTM-Youtube workload. Similarly, on the LSTM-UCF workload, our design outperforms TIE in throughput and energy efficiency while maintaining comparable area efficiency. The proposed algorithm and hardware Co-Design provides a viable solution for deploying LSTMs on resource-constrained edge devices to process video data, holding substantial value for the Internet of Video. The source code for this project is available at: https://github.com/steven-lyu/FDHT_LSTM.

R.W.K. Odoni established that for fields of characteristic zero, the Galois group of the $n$-th iterate of the generic monic polynomial of degree $d \geq 2$ corresponds to the $n$-fold iterated wreath product of the symmetric group $S_d$, a result later generalized to positive characteristic by Juul. In this work, we consider a finite field $\F_q$ where $q$ is a power of a prime $p > 2$, and let $k = \overline{\F}_q$ denote its algebraic closure. We demonstrate that for any irreducible monic polynomial $F(t,x) \in k[t][x]$ of degree $n > 0$ which is separable over $k(t)$, and a generic monic polynomial $\Phi(a_0,\dots,a_{d-1},t)$ in $t$ of degree $d \geq 2$ with algebraically independent coefficients $\mathbf a = (a_0,\dots,a_{d-1})$, the Galois group of the $m$-th iterate of the composite polynomial $F(t,\Phi(\mathbf a,t))$ over $k(a_0,\dots,a_{d-1})$ is the $m$-fold iterated wreath product of $S_{nd}$. Furthermore, applying this finding to an explicit form of the Chebotarev density theorem for function fields yields analogues of the Bateman-Horn conjecture and Chowla's conjecture regarding the autocorrelation of the Möbius function, particularly as the finite field grows large; these applications are detailed herein. The broader implications of this result beyond number theory are also discussed. Notably, the core idea driving this application of Chebotarev is an analogy between the prime specializations used by Odoni for number fields and the Frobenius specializations applicable to function fields, which we exploit extensively. This paper examines the Schrödinger equation featuring a mass-supercritical focusing nonlinearity in the region outside a smooth, compact, convex obstacle in $\R^{d}$, subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. We demonstrate that solutions possessing negative energy exhibit finite-time blow-up. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is energy-subcritical and given further symmetry constraints, we establish blow-up governed by the same optimal ground-state criterion found in Holmer and Roudenko's work on $\R^{d}$. The traditional Glassey proof, which relies on the concavity of variance, is inapplicable in the presence of an obstacle due to boundary terms arising in the second derivative of the variance that carry an unfavorable sign. To address this, our primary approach involves introducing a novel modified variance that is bounded from below and strictly concave for the specific solutions under consideration.

This work introduces a non-standard proof demonstrating that a variety, defined over the integers as the zero locus of polynomial equations, admits a local characteristic-zero semi-parametric lifting if and only if it possesses a collection of local semi-parametric reductions in positive characteristic for almost all primes, provided there exists a global complexity bound encompassing all associated structures. Such results are essential for transferring theorems from commutative algebra between characteristic-zero and positive-characteristic contexts. Notably, this proof avoids employing model theory. An explicit example illustrating the utility of this result is discussed. The presented demonstration requires a complexity assumption, specifically a global bound on the dimensions of the varieties involved at each prime; under an additional assumption, this condition can be relaxed. Furthermore, the proof does not rely on the recent work by Ayasli, Bhatt, and Pal. An appendix by J. Ayasli is included, detailing an explicit version of the result applicable to varieties defined by ideals generated by two elements.

Hypothesis testing is a fundamental component of cognitive science, with Bayes factors offering a primary method for evaluating hypotheses based on their compatibility with observed data to facilitate selection among competing models. Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical implementation remains uncertain regarding its robustness to computational details. This study examines these issues within the context of cognitive science applications. We clarify the statistical foundations of Bayes factors for Bayesian inference and emphasize the necessity of utility functions for making principled decisions. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of Bayes factors under various conditions, including errors in estimation. Notably, it remains unclear whether bridge sampling yields unbiased estimates for complex analyses; we address this by employing simulation-based calibration for the first time to assess the accuracy of such estimates. Our analysis also covers the stability of Bayes factors across different MCMC samples, their dependence on data variations, and the variability of resulting decisions, proposing methods to optimize these decisions via utility functions. We outline a reproducible workflow for researchers to test the robustness of Bayes factors in their specific analyses, illustrated with a case study from cognitive science. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a framework for evaluating the strengths and limitations of Bayes factors as a metric for scientific evidence. Reproducible code is accessible at https://osf.io/y356c/.

Discourse markers, such as {\it by contrast} and {\it happily}, are words or phrases that indicate semantic and/or pragmatic connections between clauses or sentences. Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). These inferences enable us to examine the relationship between discourse markers and the semantic relations annotated in these datasets. Although handcrafted mappings have been suggested between markers and discourse relations for limited sets of markers and categories, hundreds of discourse markers express a diverse range of relations, and there is no agreed-upon taxonomy of relations among competing theories (which are predominantly constructed top-down). By employing an automatic prediction method over existing semantically annotated datasets, we offer a bottom-up characterization of discourse markers in English. The resulting dataset, called DiscSense, is publicly accessible. Our analysis of the DiscSense dataset suggests that one semantic relation can be indicated by multiple markers and, counterintuitively, that a marker used to signal a specific relation with a particular pair of sentences may indicate a different relation with another pair. Further investigation into our dataset reveals notable differences between professional annotations of discourse relations in a corpus and those in existing datasets and between the automatic predictions on the Discourse Grounded Corpus (DGC) that align with its gold-standard labels and the rest. These findings support the view that explicit mention of a discourse marker does not always guarantee the correct labeling of the associated relation, a conclusion supported by our proposed method for identifying potential errors in discourse-structured data. Leveraging the DiscSense dataset, we provide an automatic technique for flagging potentially incorrect discourse relation annotations and offer a set of recommendations for manually annotating discourse relations in corpora. Finally, using DiscSense, we demonstrate the feasibility of classifying text classification datasets according to the discourse relations they represent and introduce two novel NLP tasks for discourse analysis that can be addressed with the DiscSense dataset. Experimental results on these tasks highlight the competitiveness of our approach. Additionally, we show how the DiscSense dataset can inform the interpretation of neural network predictions on semantically annotated datasets. Ultimately, we argue that such datasets and their analysis are essential for advancing research on discourse. Our analyses and recommendations concerning discourse relations in corpora are also relevant to pragmatic research on linguistic categories. We introduce an explicit extension of the $r$-symmetrized Jordanian twist originally formulated by Giaquinto and Zhang. We demonstrate that this generalization fulfills the 2-cocycle condition. Furthermore, we provide explicit expressions for the associated star product and twisted coproduct. Finally, we establish that our generalized twist is equivalent to the simple Jordanian twist modified by a 1-cochain. This equivalence confirms our explicit construction of the 3-cochain that defines this 1-cochain deformation. Our work offers a concrete realization of the equivalence between $r$-symmetrized and Drinfel'd-type twists, potentially serving as a valuable resource for future investigations. We do not address the relation to Lie bi-cocycles. The examples presented here generalize what is discussed in Ref. arXiv:math/0601022.

This paper introduces a novel approach to the containment problem for extended regular expressions, which incorporate intersection and complement operators, and for expressions defined over potentially infinite character sets. Unlike standard methods that fail to address extended operators or infinite alphabets, the proposed algorithm handles the complement by representing it symbolically and manages intersection by converting regular expressions into deterministic finite automata. To solve regular expression inequalities, the system employs a new technique for deciding equality between extended regular expressions. The authors present the underlying theory, detail the algorithms, and provide comprehensive proofs of correctness. Furthermore, they integrate this framework into the Prolog program CREOLE to resolve regular expression inequality problems. Extensive experiments conducted with CREOLE demonstrate the feasibility of the approach and offer comparisons against existing solutions. The source code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/hsu005/SSE. Key terms include: symbolic, solving, extended regular expressions, containment, complement, intersection, finite automata, and professional regular expressions.

Building upon the research of \cite{Ferrara:1971vh} and \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we derive an integral representation for OPE blocks associated with spinning primaries in CFT$_{2}$. We find that when these blocks are constructed from conserved spinning primaries, the integral decomposes into a product of two weighted AdS$_{2}$ field copies, smeared along geodesics. Consequently, conserved current OPE blocks in CFT$_{2}$ admit a distinct formulation via AdS$_{2}$ geodesic operators rather than the traditional AdS$_{3}$ geodesic operators. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this perspective connects to AdS$_{3}$ massless higher spin fields through HKLL bulk field reconstruction. Leveraging this framework, we successfully derive a closed-form expression for the four-point spinning conformal block.

Detecting magnetic fields with high sensitivity remains a significant challenge in metrology. In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. As anticipated, the atomic interferometry data showed a clear shift when the YBCO was cooled below $T_c$ in the 20 $\mu$T environment compared to when it was above $T_0$. Consequently, this technique offers a demonstration of sensitive magnetic field detection using a straightforward atomic interferometry configuration, which could find applications in magnetometry, and provides direct evidence of the Meissner effect through the lens of quantum mechanics. We bring together Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem (1931), Tarski's Undefinability Theorem (1933), Godel-Carnap's Diagonal Lemma (1934), and Rosser's Incompleteness Theorem (1936), which strengthens Godel's first result. These proofs share significant similarities and employ nearly identical techniques. We present unified versions of all four, arranging them in a logical sequence that culminates in Rosser's theorem. While Godel's demonstration relies on the specific nature of the $\gamma$-predicate (representing numerical satisfaction via the diagonal lemma), Rosser's approach is independent of any particular predicate, utilizing only the system's incompleteness and a clever contrapositive argument. Consequently, Rosser's theorem holds even when the diagonal lemma is no longer available, as in the language $L_{\omega,\omega}(\mathbf{D})$ discussed by Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser themselves. In this language, we derive Godel's and Rosser's incompleteness results (for arithmetic without the $\gamma$-predicate) relative to Tarski's undefinability theorem and its generalizations. Our presentation is entirely self-contained, requiring no prior knowledge of Godel's first incompleteness theorem or its context. Thus, the proof serves as an ideal starting point for an undergraduate course or competition (such as Putnam) that covers first-order logic and its extensions. Furthermore, the unified proof is highly amenable to formalization in computer systems like Coq, Leo, Isar, Agda, or Lean. We have already implemented it in Leo (by the author) and Godel.Prolog (by Schlick), achieving the earliest formalization of Godel's and Rosser's theorems in these systems without employing any of their own specialized machinery; the proof remains completely classical and self-sufficient. This characteristic makes it an excellent candidate for illustrating the formalization process itself within these environments.

This study addresses the inverse problem of identifying a source term within a structural acoustic PDE model, which consists of a two- or three-dimensional interior acoustic wave equation linked to a Kirchhoff plate equation via a boundary. While the overall setup remains linear, the proposed solution method is nonlinear and does not require prior knowledge of the problem's linearity. The approach involves a boundary term that has been logarithmically modified by an unknown initial condition, enabling the derivation of unique solutions and a priori estimates for both the initial condition and the term itself. These estimates are crucial for establishing uniqueness and are obtained without relying on complex Carleman estimates. Ultimately, a sequence of local results is established to conclude the uniqueness of the global priori estimate and the existence of a solution. Numerical experiments are included to validate the proposed method.

This study examines the coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino behavior, and dark matter properties within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale originates from tree-level seesaw dynamics, whereas the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. We pinpoint parameter regions that satisfy theoretical constraints, align with dark matter relic density, and are viable under direct detection limits. Employing two-loop renormalization group equations, we investigate vacuum stability and the consistency of the fundamental dark parity symmetry, while also deriving a lower bound for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Our analysis reveals that achieving the standard relic density via annihilation at the scale of 200 GeW is contingent upon either extending the neutral sector mass spectrum beyond 200 GeV or incorporating co-annihilation mechanisms near the dark parity breaking threshold. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both the seesaw and dark sector masses can be rooted in spontaneous breaking of the fundamental parity symmetry. Notably, we identify a region where all parameters remain below the GUT scale, ensuring stability, with the dominant neutral mediator mass lying between 2 and 10 TeV. In this specific area, the $n\nu-\text{SS}^{0}$ and $n\nu-\text{ODM}$ cross sections fall short of the targets set by Cosmic Accelerator experiments. Conversely, we highlight a region with a lighter mediator (below 2 TeV) that satisfies dark matter, direct detection, and cosmic cross-section constraints, yet remains undetectable by LHC colliders. We conclude by summarizing the key findings of this work.
